term: USERRA (The Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act)
definition: The Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act (USERRA) protects active and reserve military members from discrimination by their employers for their military participation and requires employers to rehire some employees who become deployed. USERRA’s main purpose is to prevent employers from discriminating against military employees whether it is by firing them, failing to promote them, or making their assignments more difficult than for others in similar roles. Any discriminatory action could be a violation of the Act if the military service was a “motivating factor” of the action. Employees may have different remedies such as temporary injunctions against their termination or monetary damages. Most claims are resolved administratively through the Secretary of Labor, but employees may also bring a claim in court themselves or potentially through arbitration. Another important provision requires employers to rehire most veterans after returning from service. The veteran employee must be rehired at a position and pay equal to that as if the employee had never left, and this means some employers must rehire the employees on better terms than they left. To qualify, a veteran must have given the employer proper notice of future uniformed service and must start employment again soon after finishing service. This does not apply for employees who are in uniformed service for less than 32 days. Those who are in service for 32-180 days cannot be terminated by their employer after returning for at least 180 days (with certain exceptions), and those in service for 180 days or more cannot be terminated for up to one year. There are exceptions that may disqualify an employee. An employer is not required to rehire an employee when they can prove that rehiring is no longer possible due to changes in the business or major financial difficulties preventing them from doing so. However, this does not mean the job is simply no longer available, or that the same exact job no longer exists, but that reemployment is highly impractical for the employer.
